strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a relevant clinical NLP bottleneck: access to annotated clinical text. Its 8,767 examples cover 14 SBDH categories and pain, with spans, presence, temporality, and rationales, making the resource contribution broader than several existing datasets.

The experiments support the central claim that synthetic pretraining can improve downstream classification. RoBERTa macro-F1 increases from 55.64 to 91.11 on MIMIC-SBDH aligned with prompt-based tuning, and from 72.38 to 80.71 on VA-SBDH with standard tuning. Three-run reporting, low-resource experiments, and the training-step-matched comparison against MIMIC pretraining strengthen this evidence.

The expert review of all 1,755 synthetic test examples is substantial. Adjudication, correction of missing and erroneous annotations, rationale review, and detailed error examples provide useful quality assurance and documentation of synthetic-data limitations.

The manuscript provides generation prompts, 45 seed examples, model identifiers, label mappings, training configurations, and a public repository link. These materials support reuse and make the core resource and public-dataset experiments a contribution suitable for Findings.
weaknesses: The headline improvements require qualification. The 94.44-point housing-insecurity improvement rests on only 18 positive test examples, so variation across training seeds understates uncertainty from test sampling. The largest NER improvement comes from an unstable T5 baseline (25.44 ± 18.24 macro-F1); encoder NER gains are negligible, and several Mamba/Llama settings show no improvement. Class-balancing and matched additional-training controls would better establish the advantage behind these effects.

The generalization evidence has a limited scope. Both clinical evaluations include supervised adaptation to the target dataset, and the seed examples and definitions originate from the VA setting. Synthetic examples are substantially shorter than the real examples. Experiments also merge categories, discard overlapping annotations, and do not directly evaluate temporal or presence-attribute extraction, leaving parts of the advertised annotation richness unvalidated.

The reasoning-distillation claim exceeds the evidence. DSS improves macro-F1 by only 0.66 and 0.58 points on the synthetic test set, with the FLAN-T5 result nonsignificant (P=0.36). This establishes limited evidence for an auxiliary rationale-training benefit, without demonstrating transferred reasoning capability. Testing extraction on real clinical data would not require reference rationales at evaluation time.

The expert audit does not fully establish an independent gold standard. Annotators inspect GPT-4 outputs, and Appendix E.2 explicitly permits retaining GPT-4's choice among plausible categories while applying a different preference when adding annotations. Moreover, the 71.06% agreement includes missing annotations in its denominator, whereas GPT-4's 90.78% self-evaluation excludes them. Clearer metric definitions, comparable denominators, and attribute-specific agreement would improve confidence in benchmark quality.

Reporting and reproducibility need tightening. The reported split sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767, and several Llama 3.2 results in Table 14 exactly repeat ClinicalMamba values from Table 3 and warrant verification. Exact downstream prompts/verbalizers and generation decoding settings are not specified in the manuscript, while the private VA dataset limits independent replication. Together with the restricted evidence for broader claims, these issues limit confidence in a main-conference recommendation.
